claims.text: Untreated Q235 steel rapidly forms a surface oxide scale during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The high-temperature scale on Q235 likely contains Fe3O4 and/or related spinel phases.
A sufficiently adherent and continuous oxide scale governs corrosion protection by slowing further degradation.
At room temperature, oxide-formation kinetics are too slow to produce a comparably protective scale on Q235.
Failure to form a comparable protective scale at room temperature produces higher local corrosion rates.
Pre-annealing Q235 promotes formation of a protective oxide scale.
Increasing temperature accelerates oxidation and produces a faster, more uniform, and more adherent scale.
The oxide scale limits elemental dissolution and mass loss from the steel.
Elemental dissolution can cause mass loss during high-temperature molten-salt corrosion.
Sufficient oxygen availability is required for significant formation of the proposed protective scale.
The proposed protective-scale mechanism applies primarily during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C and not at ambient temperature or low oxygen availability.
High-temperature Q235 specimens will exhibit a coherent oxide scale detectable by XRD and SEM/EDS.
Formation of the coherent scale will correspond to reduced net mass change and lower corrosion rates relative to conditions where the scale does not form.
High-temperature microstructural or phase evolution can depend on exposure temperature and duration.
The protective quality and exact composition of the Q235 oxide scale may depend on salt composition, exposure time, and local microstructural heterogeneity.
Scanning Kelvin probe analysis can assess relative electron work-function variations associated with local electrochemical activity.

contradictions.description: The focal specimen is explicitly untreated and therefore lacks induced pre-annealing, but the predicted outcome compares untreated high-temperature Q235 against 'samples without induced pre-annealing.' This makes the test specimen and one stated comparator the same treatment class.

The pre-annealed reference is intended to promote oxide formation, yet similarity between untreated high-temperature samples and the reference is treated as evidence of falsification. Similarity could instead mean that both developed the proposed protective scale, so this comparison is not intrinsically falsifying.
